name: Athanasius of Alexandria
summary: Bishop of Alexandria who spent nearly half a century defending the Nicene teaching that the Son is fully God against Arianism, enduring five exiles under four emperors.

key_dates.label: Attends the Council of Nicaea as deacon and secretary to Bishop Alexander
Deposed by the Council of Tyre; first exile, to Trier
Third exile; hides among the monks of the Egyptian desert
Fourth exile, ordered by Emperor Julian
Fifth and last exile, under Emperor Valens
39th Festal Letter lists the 27 books of the New Testament

accomplishments.text: Defended the Nicene Creed's teaching that the Son is "of one substance" (homoousios) with the Father against Arius and his successors for nearly fifty years, often almost alone among leading bishops.
Wrote On the Incarnation, a classic explanation of why God became human, and the Orations against the Arians.
Wrote the Life of Antony (c. 360), a biography of the desert hermit that spread the ideal of monasticism across the Roman world.
In his 39th Festal Letter (367), gave the first known list of exactly the 27 books now in the New Testament.
Built close ties with the Egyptian monks, who sheltered him during his exiles.
Is honored as a saint and Church Father in Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, and Lutheran churches, and as a Doctor of the Church in the Catholic Church.

misattributed.phrase: The Athanasian Creed ("Whosoever will be saved…")
misattributed.note: This creed bears his name but was written in Latin, probably in southern Gaul in the late 5th or 6th century, long after his death.

misattributed.reference: A later description of him, not his words
misattributed.note: A later Latin phrase summing up his lonely stand, not something he said.

persecution_note: Athanasius was exiled five times by four emperors, spending about seventeen of his forty-five years as bishop away from his see. He was repeatedly condemned by councils of bishops on the Arian or compromise side, and on one occasion soldiers broke into his church to seize him. He was never executed and died as bishop in Alexandria.

persecution.title: Deposed at Tyre; first exile to Trier
persecution.summary: His opponents accused him of violence against his clergy and even of murdering a bishop named Arsenius, who later turned up alive. The Council of Tyre, dominated by his opponents, deposed him. Emperor Constantine, after being told that Athanasius had threatened to stop Egypt's grain shipments to Constantinople, exiled him to Trier in Gaul.

responsible.name: Council of Tyre
responsible.jurisdiction: Synod of eastern bishops convened by Constantine

responsible.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
responsible.role: Leader of the pro-Arian party that pressed the charges

persecution.outcome: Allowed to return after Constantine's death in 337.

persecution.title: Second exile; replaced by Gregory of Cappadocia
persecution.summary: Emperor Constantius II, who favored the anti-Nicene bishops, had Gregory of Cappadocia installed as bishop of Alexandria by force. Athanasius fled to Rome.

responsible.name: Emperor Constantius II
responsible.role: Backed his removal and the installation of a rival bishop

defended_by.name: Pope Julius I
defended_by.role: Bishop of Rome; received him and declared him innocent at a council in Rome (341)

defended_by.name: Emperor Constans
defended_by.role: Western emperor who pressed his brother Constantius to restore him

persecution.outcome: Restored in 346 after Gregory's death, under pressure from the western emperor Constans.

persecution.title: Soldiers storm his church; third exile
persecution.summary: After the councils of Arles (353) and Milan (355) condemned him under imperial pressure, troops under the military commander Syrianus broke into the Church of Theonas during a night vigil to arrest him. He escaped and hid for six years among the desert monks, while George of Cappadocia was installed as bishop.

responsible.name: Syrianus
responsible.role: Military commander (dux) of Egypt; led the raid on the church

responsible.name: George of Cappadocia
responsible.role: Installed as bishop of Alexandria in his place

defended_by.name: Pope Liberius
defended_by.role: Refused to condemn him and was exiled for it (355), although he later wavered

persecution.outcome: He returned in 362 after Constantius's death.

persecution.title: Fourth exile, under Julian the Apostate
persecution.summary: The pagan emperor Julian, who had allowed exiled bishops to return, banished Athanasius again after he converted prominent pagans in Alexandria, calling him an enemy of the gods.

persecution.title: Fifth exile, under Valens
persecution.summary: Emperor Valens, who favored the anti-Nicene party, ordered bishops exiled under Constantius to be expelled again. Athanasius hid for about four months, reportedly in his family's tomb outside the city.
persecution.outcome: Recalled in 366, apparently to avoid unrest in Alexandria. He remained bishop until his death in 373.

excommunication_note: Athanasius was deposed and condemned several times by councils of bishops, mostly on the Arian or compromise side. All of these sentences were overturned or ignored, and he died in possession of his see. He is venerated as a saint in all major traditions.

excommunications.authority: Synod of eastern bishops convened by Emperor Constantine
excommunications.reason: Deposed on charges of violence and misconduct brought by his opponents
excommunications.status: Overturned; restored in 337 and later vindicated by Rome and the western bishops

excommunications.by: Eastern bishops meeting at Philippopolis (the eastern half of the Council of Serdica)
excommunications.reason: Condemned Athanasius and also excommunicated Pope Julius I for supporting him
excommunications.status: Rejected by the western bishops at Serdica

excommunications.authority: Western synods acting under Emperor Constantius II
excommunications.reason: Bishops were required to sign his condemnation; those who refused were exiled
